techniques.when_to_use: Default between retrieval and generation; most valuable when k is large, contexts exceed a few thousand tokens, per-token cost matters, or the generator is a small/chat-sized model prone to position bias.
techniques.tradeoffs: RECOMP keeps 5-10% of tokens at <=~10% relative loss (NQ EM 39.39 -> 37.04 with 660 -> 36 tokens); LongLLMLingua gains +21.4% on NQ with ~4x fewer tokens and 1.4-2.6x latency speedup. Abstractive compression lowers citation recall (ALCE SUMM: 73.6 -> 68.9) and risks paraphrase errors on numbers; extractive is safer for specs and code.
techniques.default_parameters: Budget B = 2,000-4,000 tokens of evidence for chat-sized models (RAPTOR used a 2,000-token collapsed-tree budget ~ top-20 nodes). Extractive: top-1 sentence per chunk for single-hop, top-2 for multi-hop (RECOMP). Compression ratio 2x-6x for prose (LongLLMLingua), 1x (none) for code/tables. Ordering: best-first, second-best-last, remainder in the middle. Empty-evidence passthrough enabled.

techniques.name: Iterative retrieval loop for multi-hop and long-form tasks (IRCoT + FLARE)
techniques.description: For MULTI_STEP plans: initialize context with the fused top chunks; loop up to S steps: generate one reasoning step (CoT sentence or sub-answer); if the step contains low-confidence tokens (logprob below tau) or an explicit 'need more info' marker, use the step text (or a generated sub-question) as a new retrieval query, retrieve top-k, dedupe into context, and regenerate the step; stop when the model emits a final answer or the step budget is exhausted. For long-form generation (reports, postmortems), apply the same loop per paragraph/section (FLARE) rather than per reasoning step. Each hop is logged with its query, retrieved IDs and confidence for traceability.
source_titles: Interleaving Retrieval with Chain-of-Thought Reasoning for Knowledge-Intensive Multi-Step Questions (IRCoT)
Active Retrieval Augmented Generation (FLARE)
Adaptive-RAG: Learning to Adapt Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models through Question Complexity
techniques.when_to_use: Questions needing evidence from multiple documents/components (trace a requirement to tests to incidents), root-cause analysis across logs, and long-form synthesis where information needs emerge during writing.
techniques.tradeoffs: Latency and cost scale with hops: Adaptive-RAG's multi-step averaged 2.1-4.7 retrieval rounds and 3.3-8.8x single-step time. Gains: IRCoT +21 points retrieval and +15 points QA on HotpotQA/2Wiki/MuSiQue/IIRC. Risk of query drift and runaway loops without a budget.
techniques.default_parameters: Max steps S=4 (observed averages 2-5); k=4-8 new chunks per hop with dedupe; FLARE confidence threshold tau on min token probability around 0.4-0.8 (tune on validation; lower tau retrieves less); stop on a final-answer marker; total token budget enforced across hops.

techniques.name: Hierarchical and graph indexing for document- and corpus-level questions (RAPTOR + GraphRAG)
techniques.description: Build two auxiliary indexes alongside chunk vectors. RAPTOR tree: leaf chunks ~100 tokens; embed; reduce with UMAP; cluster with GMM (BIC-selected cluster count, soft membership); summarize each cluster with a cheap LLM; recurse until one root; store every node in the vector index with a level tag; query with the collapsed-tree strategy (search all levels, take nodes by score within a 2,000-token budget). GraphRAG: extract entities/relations per 600-token chunk with 1-2 gleaning passes; build a graph; Leiden community detection to produce hierarchical communities C0 (root) to C3; pre-generate community reports; answer GLOBAL plan queries by map (score each community report's partial answer) and reduce (synthesize top partial answers). The router sends 'what are the themes/risks across X' to GraphRAG, 'what does this document say about Y' to RAPTOR collapsed tree, and precise lookups to chunk retrieval.
source_titles: RAPTOR: Recursive Abstractive Processing for Tree-Organized Retrieval
From Local to Global: A Graph RAG Approach to Query-Focused Summarization
Retrieval meets Long Context Large Language Models
techniques.when_to_use: Long technical documents (specifications, standards, design docs) and corpus-wide sensemaking (patterns across incident reports, cross-cutting requirements), where chunk retrieval fails on 'general' and 'implicit whole-context' queries (Li et al.'s RAG failure categories).
techniques.tradeoffs: Indexing cost is high (LLM summarization of every cluster/community; GraphRAG entity extraction over every chunk) and must be re-run on corpus change. Query cost at C0 is 9-43x lower than source-text map-reduce. Gains: RAPTOR+GPT-4 QuALITY 82.6% vs 62.3% prior best; GraphRAG 72-83% win rate on comprehensiveness. Summaries can hallucinate; keep provenance links to leaf chunks.
techniques.default_parameters: RAPTOR: leaf chunk 100 tokens, GMM with UMAP, collapsed-tree retrieval with 2,000-token budget (~top-20 nodes). GraphRAG: 600-token chunks, 100-token overlap, 1 gleaning pass (more for recall-critical corpora), Leiden hierarchy, default query level C1/C2 (C0 for cheap overviews, C3 for detail). Rebuild incrementally per document delta.

techniques.name: Citation-grounded generation with NLI verification
techniques.description: The generation prompt requires every factual statement to carry one or more citation markers [n] referring to evidence units in context (which carry source-span pointers back through compression). Post-generation: split the answer into statements; for each statement, run an NLI/entailment judge (TRUE-style T5-11B or an LLM judge) over the concatenated cited passages; citation recall = fraction of statements entailed by their citations; citation precision = fraction of citations individually necessary (a citation is irrelevant if it does not entail the statement alone and removing it leaves the rest still entailing). Statements failing recall are regenerated with a constrained prompt or flagged/removed; precision failures prune superfluous citations. Also compute RAGAS faithfulness (statement-level support against all context) as a cheaper proxy.
source_titles: Enabling Large Language Models to Generate Text with Citations (ALCE)
Self-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection
RAGAs: Automated Evaluation of Retrieval Augmented Generation
techniques.when_to_use: Any answer a human will act on (compliance, safety, engineering decisions) and any output that will be audited; mandatory when the pipeline feeds downstream automated steps.
techniques.tradeoffs: One NLI pass per statement (batchable, ~tens of ms each with a cross-encoder; one LLM call with a judge). Even strong models lack full citation support ~50% of the time on long-form ELI5 (ALCE), so expect regeneration overhead. Compression lowers citation recall; interactive 'check the full passage' did not help ChatGPT (ALCE INTERACT).
techniques.default_parameters: Top-5 full passages (ALCE main setting) or up to 20 compressed evidence units for GPT-4-class models; require >=1 citation per factual statement; release gate at citation recall >= 0.8 and faithfulness >= 0.9 on sampled traffic (RAGAS faithfulness agrees with humans at 0.95); maximum one regeneration round per statement.

techniques.name: Reference-free evaluation triad with calibrated judges (RAGAS + ARES + failure-point telemetry)
techniques.description: Offline: generate synthetic in-domain QA from the corpus (FLAN-T5-class or an LLM), filtered so the retriever returns the source passage at rank 1, with weak and strong negatives; fine-tune or prompt judges for context relevance, faithfulness and answer relevance; collect 150-300 human labels per domain and apply prediction-powered inference to produce confidence intervals and rank pipeline configurations. Online: sample N% of traffic, compute the RAGAS triad plus gold-in-top-k (when feedback exists), abstention rate, schema-validation failures, latency, and token cost; attribute every failure to Barnett's FP1-FP7; alert on drift; feed labeled failures back into router and retriever training. Evaluate position sensitivity by permuting gold-passage position on the validation set.
source_titles: RAGAs: Automated Evaluation of Retrieval Augmented Generation
ARES: An Automated Evaluation Framework for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
Seven Failure Points When Engineering a Retrieval Augmented Generation System
Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts
techniques.when_to_use: From day one of any production deployment; 'validation is only feasible during operation' (Barnett), so offline benchmarks alone are insufficient.
techniques.tradeoffs: Judge calls add cost (sample rather than evaluate 100%); RAGAS context relevance is the least reliable metric (0.70 human agreement); ARES needs ~150 labels but yields Kendall tau 0.91-0.97 and intervals. Synthetic data can mirror the generator's biases.
techniques.default_parameters: Sample 5-10% of production traffic for judge scoring; 150-300 human labels per domain for PPI calibration (ARES); release thresholds: faithfulness >= 0.9, answer relevance >= 0.8, citation recall >= 0.8, abstention rate within an expected band; compute failure-point attribution weekly; re-run position-sensitivity test on every generator model change.

techniques.name: Distractor-aware generator fine-tuning (RAFT / Yoran et al. / Wang et al. best-practices recipe)
techniques.description: For deployments hosting an open-weight generator: (1) generate synthetic QA pairs from the corpus (one question per chunk, answer grounded in that chunk, optionally with a chain-of-thought that quotes verbatim spans); (2) for each example build a context of the oracle chunk plus k-1 top-ranked distractors retrieved for the same question, and for a fraction p of examples omit the oracle entirely so the model learns to abstain or answer from parametric knowledge; (3) fine-tune (LoRA is sufficient) with the target being the quoted-span chain-of-thought answer; (4) evaluate on held-out questions with all-noise contexts and relevant contexts separately to confirm robustness without loss.
source_titles: RAFT: Adapting Language Model to Domain Specific RAG
Making Retrieval-Augmented Language Models Robust to Irrelevant Context
Searching for Best Practices in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
Chain-of-Note: Enhancing Robustness in Retrieval-Augmented Language Models
techniques.when_to_use: When weights are tunable and retrieval noise is a measured failure cause (Barnett FP4), or when a small model must replace a frontier API for cost; especially for narrow engineering domains where the base model's prior is weak.
techniques.tradeoffs: Requires an offline synthetic data pipeline and periodic retraining when the corpus or chunking changes; risk of overfitting to synthetic question style. Yoran et al. reached robustness with about 1,000 examples; RAFT consistently improved over RAG baselines on PubMed/HotpotQA/Gorilla; Wang et al. found random-document mixing produced the most robust generator.
techniques.default_parameters: Mix roughly 50-80% examples with oracle + 4 distractors and 20-50% with distractors only (RAFT explores p in this range); about 1,000-5,000 examples per domain (Yoran et al.: ~1,000 suffice); LoRA on a 7-8B model; include verbatim quotes and citation markers in the target; retrain on major corpus or chunking changes.

techniques.name: LLM listwise reranking with sliding window and permutation distillation (RankGPT)
techniques.description: After hybrid fusion, present candidates in windows of w passages (ids plus truncated text) to an LLM with an instruction to output a permutation of ids by relevance; slide the window from the bottom of the list upward with stride s so top candidates bubble up; take the final top-k. To make this production-cheap, log the LLM permutations over production queries and distill them into a small cross-encoder or listwise model with a RankNet-style loss, then swap the LLM reranker for the distilled model and keep the LLM as an offline teacher.
source_titles: Is ChatGPT Good at Search? Investigating Large Language Models as Re-Ranking Agents (RankGPT)
Introducing Contextual Retrieval
Searching for Best Practices in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
techniques.when_to_use: When no in-domain reranker exists or domain shift makes off-the-shelf cross-encoders unreliable; at cold start of a new corpus; as a teacher for training a cheap domain reranker.
techniques.tradeoffs: LLM reranking costs several LLM calls per query (window count) and 1-3 s latency, so it is not a steady-state choice for 150 candidates; distilled models lose a little quality but RankGPT's 440M distilled model beat a 3B supervised reranker on BEIR. Permutation parsing can fail and needs repair logic.
techniques.default_parameters: Window w=20, stride s=10, rerank the top 100 fused candidates to select top 20; temperature 0; truncate passages to ~300 tokens inside the prompt. Distill once 10k+ query-permutation pairs exist; then use the distilled reranker for 150 -> 20 and keep LLM reranking as an escalation for AMBIGUOUS gate outcomes.

techniques.name: Multi-granularity indexing: proposition/sentence retrieval with parent-chunk expansion (small-to-big) and late chunking
techniques.description: At indexing time produce two linked granularities: (a) retrieval units that are small and self-contained (LLM-extracted propositions as in Dense X, or contextualized sentences), each storing a pointer to its parent chunk and document; (b) parent chunks used for generation. Embed the small units (optionally with late chunking so each unit vector is computed from the full-document token embeddings). At query time retrieve top-n small units, dedupe by parent, expand to parent chunks (or a window around the unit), and pass the parents, with the matched units highlighted, to the gate/compressor. Citations resolve to the small unit's span.
source_titles: Dense X Retrieval: What Retrieval Granularity Should We Use?
Late Chunking: Contextual Chunk Embeddings Using Long-Context Embedding Models
Introducing Contextual Retrieval
RECOMP: Improving Retrieval-Augmented LMs with Context Compression and Selective Augmentation
techniques.when_to_use: When questions target specific facts inside long, multi-topic chunks (specs, standards), when chunk-level retrieval shows low precision, or when citation granularity must be a sentence or clause.
techniques.tradeoffs: Proposition extraction is an LLM pass over the corpus (comparable to contextual retrieval cost) and multiplies vector count 5-10x; late chunking requires a long-context embedding model and does not help BM25. Dense X reports significant retrieval gains over passage units and better QA under a fixed token budget; Qu et al. caution that chunking changes must be validated on the actual corpus.
techniques.default_parameters: Retrieval unit: proposition or sentence (20-80 tokens) with 50-100-token contextual prefix; parent chunk 256-512 tokens; retrieve top-50 units, expand to at most 20 parents; store parent_id, span offsets and document version on every unit; use late chunking when corpus size makes per-chunk LLM prefixes unaffordable.

techniques.name: Knowledge-conflict consolidation with source-tracked claims (Astute RAG)
techniques.description: Before final generation: (1) elicit the model's own answer and supporting claims from parametric knowledge (bounded to a few sentences, labeled as internal); (2) extract claims from each retrieved passage with source ids; (3) iteratively consolidate claims into groups that agree, disagree or are independent, keeping the list of sources per group and noting document version/date; (4) score each group by number and reliability of sources (internal knowledge gets a configurable low weight); (5) generate the answer from the highest-reliability consistent group, and explicitly surface unresolved conflicts (e.g. two spec revisions disagree) instead of choosing silently; (6) if no group reaches the reliability threshold, abstain or escalate.
source_titles: Astute RAG: Overcoming Imperfect Retrieval Augmentation and Knowledge Conflicts for Large Language Models
The Power of Noise: Redefining Retrieval for RAG Systems
Benchmarking Large Language Models in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RGB)
techniques.when_to_use: Corpora with multiple document revisions, overlapping sources (wiki vs spec vs ticket) or user-contributed content; any domain where counterfactual or stale evidence is plausible and where answers must disclose disagreement.
techniques.tradeoffs: Adds one or two LLM calls and more output tokens; internal-knowledge elicitation can inject hallucinations if weighted too high. Astute RAG was the only method matching or beating the non-RAG LLM in the worst-case all-noise setting; RGB shows counterfactual robustness is among the weakest LLM abilities, so this step addresses a measured gap.
techniques.default_parameters: One consolidation iteration by default (Astute RAG uses a small fixed number); internal-knowledge weight 0.3-0.5 relative to a retrieved source; reliability score = sum of source trust weights, with newer document versions weighted higher; conflict disclosure mandatory when two groups each have at least one trusted source; abstain if top group has zero retrieved sources and citations are required.

techniques.name: Speculative drafting: parallel small-model drafts over evidence subsets with large-model verification
techniques.description: Given the gated evidence set: (1) cluster documents by embedding into m groups and sample one document per cluster to form n diverse subsets of size m; (2) in parallel, a small specialist drafter (fine-tuned or prompted 7-8B model) produces an answer draft plus rationale for each subset; (3) the large generalist model does not generate; it scores each draft by its conditional likelihood of the draft given the subset (self-consistency) and of a reflection statement such as 'the rationale supports the answer' (self-reflection); (4) select the highest-scoring draft (optionally verify citations with NLI) and return it with its subset as evidence. Falls back to standard generation when drafts disagree beyond a threshold.
source_titles: Speculative RAG: Enhancing Retrieval Augmented Generation through Drafting
REPLUG: Retrieval-Augmented Black-Box Language Models
Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts
techniques.when_to_use: High-volume SINGLE_STEP traffic where frontier-model generation dominates cost or latency; when evidence sets are large and diverse; when a capable small model is available.
techniques.tradeoffs: Requires hosting a drafter and a scoring pass that needs logprob access to the verifier (not all APIs expose it); diversity sampling can drop the single gold document from every subset. Reported gains: up to +12.97% accuracy and 50.83% lower latency vs conventional RAG on PubHealth.
techniques.default_parameters: n=5 drafts of m=2 documents (paper explores 1-10 drafts, 1-4 docs each; 5x2 is a reasonable start); drafter temperature 0.7 for diversity, verifier scoring at temperature 0; fallback to standard generation if the top two draft scores differ by less than a small margin or if drafts have no overlapping answer.

techniques.name: Retrieval-content security controls: data/instruction separation, poisoning defenses and provenance
techniques.description: (1) Ingestion: record provenance (source system, author, write permission class, timestamp, hash) per document; compute per-source trust weights; scan chunks for instruction-like patterns (imperatives addressed to assistants, hidden text, encoded payloads) and quarantine; detect near-duplicate or anomalous embeddings clustered around likely target queries (PoisonedRAG inserts a handful of texts optimized to rank first) and flag sources that suddenly dominate top-k for many queries. (2) Prompting: wrap each evidence unit in typed delimiters or spotlighting markers with an instruction hierarchy stating that evidence is data and may not change the task; never pass raw retrieved text into tool-call arguments without validation. (3) Agentic wrapper: tool permissions are decided by the TaskSpec, not by content; any tool call whose arguments originate in retrieved text requires policy approval. (4) Monitoring: detect answers whose cited sources have low trust or recent write time; keep per-answer evidence logs so poisoned documents can be traced and all affected answers invalidated.
source_titles: Not what you've signed up for: Compromising Real-World LLM-Integrated Applications with Indirect Prompt Injection
PoisonedRAG: Knowledge Corruption Attacks to Retrieval-Augmented Generation of Large Language Models
Corrective Retrieval Augmented Generation (CRAG)
techniques.when_to_use: Always in multi-tenant or user-writable corpora (wikis, tickets, shared drives, email), whenever a web-search fallback is enabled, and whenever the pipeline can trigger tools or downstream automation.
techniques.tradeoffs: Adds ingestion latency and false-positive quarantines; delimiter-based separation reduces but does not eliminate injection (Greshake et al. note defenses are lacking); trust weighting can suppress legitimate new sources. PoisonedRAG achieves ~90% attack success with five injected texts among millions, so the controls must assume successful injection and focus on blast-radius limits and traceability.
techniques.default_parameters: Trust tiers: controlled docs (1.0), internal wiki/tickets (0.7), web fallback (0.3); quarantine chunks with instruction-pattern score above threshold for human review; alert when a single new document appears in top-5 for more than N distinct queries per day; evidence delimiters plus system-prompt instruction hierarchy on every generation; tool calls allowed only from a TaskSpec whitelist with argument validation.

techniques.name: Fine-grained claim-level diagnostics and robustness test suites (RAGChecker / FActScore / RGB)
techniques.description: Build one shared claim extractor (atomic fact decomposition as in FActScore) and one entailment checker, then compute: retriever metrics (claim recall: fraction of gold-answer claims present in retrieved context; context precision: fraction of chunks containing a gold claim) and generator metrics (context utilization: fraction of retrieved gold claims used; noise sensitivity: fraction of answer claims that are wrong and traceable to retrieved chunks, split into relevant vs irrelevant chunks; hallucination rate: wrong claims not in any chunk; self-knowledge: correct claims not in any chunk; faithfulness). Complement with RGB-style robustness suites built from in-domain questions: noise-injected contexts, unanswerable contexts (negative rejection), multi-document integration questions and counterfactual-evidence variants, each scored separately per generator model.
source_titles: RAGChecker: A Fine-grained Framework for Diagnosing Retrieval-Augmented Generation
FActScore: Fine-grained Atomic Evaluation of Factual Precision in Long Form Text Generation
Benchmarking Large Language Models in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RGB)
Seven Failure Points When Engineering a Retrieval Augmented Generation System
techniques.when_to_use: Offline regression testing and sampled online evaluation whenever the pipeline has more than one stage that could be at fault; mandatory when choosing between retriever and generator upgrades, and before every generator model change.
techniques.tradeoffs: Needs reference answers (synthetic or human) for recall-type metrics, and a checker LLM per sample (cost scales with claims); claim extraction is itself noisy. RAGChecker reports higher human correlation than prior metrics; FActScore's estimator is within 2% of human judgments; RGB found negative rejection and counterfactual detection to be the weakest abilities across six LLMs.
techniques.default_parameters: Sample 5-10% of traffic for claim-level scoring; 200-500 reference questions per domain for offline suites with four RGB variants each; alert if noise sensitivity in irrelevant chunks rises above baseline by a configured margin or negative-rejection rate falls below 0.8; recompute after every retriever, chunking or generator change.

techniques.name: Graph-walk single-step multi-hop retrieval (HippoRAG Personalized PageRank)
techniques.description: Indexing: for each passage, extract (subject, relation, object) triples with an LLM (open information extraction), normalize entity names, link synonyms by embedding similarity, and build a graph whose nodes are entities (with edges to the passages they appear in). Query: extract named entities from the query, map them to graph nodes, run Personalized PageRank seeded on those nodes (optionally weighted by node specificity, i.e. inverse passage frequency), aggregate node scores to passages, and return the top-k passages in one retrieval call. Can be combined with IRCoT (use PPR retrieval inside each hop) when questions need reasoning beyond entity connectivity.
source_titles: HippoRAG: Neurobiologically Inspired Long-Term Memory for Large Language Models
Interleaving Retrieval with Chain-of-Thought Reasoning for Knowledge-Intensive Multi-Step Questions (IRCoT)
From Local to Global: A Graph RAG Approach to Query-Focused Summarization
techniques.when_to_use: Multi-entity 'connect A to B' questions (requirement to test to incident traces, component dependency chains) where iterative retrieval is too slow or costly; corpora with rich entity structure or existing traceability links that can seed the graph.
techniques.tradeoffs: Indexing requires an LLM extraction pass over every passage (similar to GraphRAG) and graph maintenance on updates; entity linking errors propagate. HippoRAG matched or beat IRCoT while 10-30x cheaper and 6-13x faster and improved multi-hop QA by up to 20% over SOTA RAG.
techniques.default_parameters: PPR damping 0.5 (HippoRAG default), synonym edge threshold cosine ~0.8, node specificity weighting on; retrieve top-5 to top-10 passages per call; router sends queries with two or more distinct entities to this retriever; seed graph edges from structured traceability data where available to skip LLM extraction.

techniques.name: Order-preserving context packing as an alternative ordering policy (OP-RAG)
techniques.description: After reranking and gating, instead of ordering chunks by relevance (best first, second best last), sort the selected chunks by (document_id, original position) so that chunks from the same document appear contiguous and in source order, inserting section headers or ellipsis markers between non-adjacent chunks. Sweep the number of retrieved chunks on a validation set to find the inverted-U optimum for the target model, since quality rises then falls as more chunks are added. Make the policy a DomainProfile setting and select it per plan: relevance-edges for multi-document fact lookups, document-order for single-document procedural or long-form questions.
source_titles: In Defense of RAG in the Era of Long-Context Language Models (OP-RAG)
Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts
Searching for Best Practices in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
techniques.when_to_use: Single-document or few-document questions over procedural or narrative sources (specifications, runbooks, postmortems) where coherence and causal order matter; long-context generators where relevance ordering fragments the narrative.
techniques.tradeoffs: Loses the 'best evidence at the edges' effect for chat-sized models with strong position bias; needs per-model tuning of chunk count. OP-RAG reported higher answer quality than full-document long-context input at a fraction of the tokens on long-context QA benchmarks; Wang et al. found 'reverse' (relevance ascending) repacking best in their ablation, so the right policy is model- and task-dependent.
techniques.default_parameters: Chunk size 128-256 tokens for OP-RAG style packing; sweep k in {8, 16, 32, 64} on validation and pick the inverted-U peak (paper found mid-range k optimal); default to relevance-edges ordering for multi-document plans and document-order for single-document plans; re-run the position-sensitivity test on every generator change.

architecture_recommendations: 1. Model the component as a typed execution graph with four control-flow primitives (linear, conditional, branching+fusion, bounded loop) per Modular RAG; every published method (Self-RAG, CRAG, FLARE, IRCoT, RAPTOR, GraphRAG) is then a declarative sub-graph/configuration, not new code. Ship a YAML/JSON 'recipe' format and a registry of operators (rewriter, retriever, fuser, reranker, gate, compressor, generator, verifier, judge).

2. Put a planner/router at the entry: it parses the natural-language task prompt into a structured TaskSpec (intent, answer format, domain, required evidence types, cost/latency tier, citation requirement) and selects a plan among NO_RETRIEVAL, SINGLE_STEP, MULTI_STEP, GLOBAL, LONG_CONTEXT. Start with an LLM-labeled router; replace with a distilled 60M-770M classifier trained on production traces (Adaptive-RAG). Always allow explicit abstention and upward escalation (Self-Route).

3. Separate indexing from serving. Indexing pipeline: structure-aware chunking (respect headings, code blocks, tables, requirement IDs), contextual prefix generation, dual indexing (BM25 + dense), metadata schema, optional RAPTOR tree and GraphRAG communities, all versioned behind aliases so embedding/chunking changes can be blue/green re-indexed (Barnett).

4. Retrieval stage defaults: parallel BM25 + dense with metadata pre-filters, RRF k=60 fusion, rerank 150 -> 20, evidence cap aligned with the reader-saturation point (~20) and the model's context size. Make retriever adapters pluggable (vector DB, search engine, SQL/metadata store, code-symbol index, ticketing API) behind one interface returning (text, source_span, metadata, score).

5. Insert a corrective evidence gate between rerank and generation (CRAG three-way decision with calibrated thresholds, configurable fallback retriever) and a selective-augmentation compressor (RECOMP-style: may return nothing) with position-aware ordering (LongLLMLingua, Lost in the Middle). Every compressed unit must keep a pointer to its original span.

6. Generation stage: prompt templates that (a) state evidence may be irrelevant and must be ignored if so (RA-DIT lesson), (b) require per-statement citations, (c) enforce output schema (JSON/Markdown/table) with validation and one repair retry (Barnett FP5), (d) expose temperature, max evidence, and persona/domain system prompts as configuration.

7. Verification stage: statement splitting, NLI-based citation recall/precision (ALCE), Self-RAG-style IsSup/IsUse judgments with configurable soft weights or hard filters; unsupported statements are regenerated or removed; abstention when nothing is supported.

8. Observability as a first-class module: trace every request (plan, queries, retrieved IDs and ranks, gate decisions, compression ratio, tokens, latency, judge scores, citations), attribute failures to FP1-FP7, sample traffic for RAGAS/ARES scoring, and store traces as training data for router, retriever and gate recalibration.

9. Cost controls: corpus-size gate (<200K tokens -> cached whole-corpus prompt, no retrieval), step and token budgets per plan, semantic/exact caching of rewrites, retrievals and final answers keyed on normalized query + index version, and model tiering (small model for routing/gating/compression, frontier model for synthesis).

10. Domain adapters: a DomainProfile object bundles chunking rules, metadata schema, retriever weights, gate thresholds, compression policy (extractive for code/specs, abstractive for prose), citation strictness and judge prompts; engineering profiles (code, requirements, standards, test logs, incidents, CAD/BOM) are shipped as presets and overridden per deployment.

11. Agentic wrapper with governance: the planner may call retrieval operators as tools in a bounded loop (max steps, max tokens, deterministic fallbacks), writes an audit log, and can hand off to task-decomposition and verification components through the same TaskSpec/Evidence/Answer message types (Singh et al. governance gaps).

12. Evaluation harness in CI: synthetic in-domain QA generation with hard negatives, 150-300 human labels per domain for PPI calibration, regression suites for retrieval recall@k, position-sensitivity, faithfulness, citation recall/precision, abstention correctness, latency and cost per plan; block releases on threshold regressions.

Security: treat every retrieved chunk as untrusted input (Greshake et al.). Wrap evidence in typed delimiters with an explicit instruction hierarchy, forbid tool calls whose arguments derive from retrieved text unless validated against a TaskSpec whitelist, scan and quarantine instruction-like or hidden content at ingestion, and sandbox the CRAG web-search fallback (no credentials, read-only, separate trust tier).

Corpus integrity: assume poisoning is feasible (PoisonedRAG: ~90% success with five injected texts). Record provenance and write-permission class per document, assign per-source trust weights that feed the evidence gate and consolidation step, alert when a newly written document starts dominating top-k across many queries, and keep per-answer evidence logs so affected answers can be identified and invalidated when a poisoned source is removed.

Observability schema: emit one structured trace per request with spans for router, each query variant, each retriever call (query, filters, index version, candidate ids and scores), fusion, rerank, gate decision and scores, compression ratio and dropped spans, generation (model, tokens, latency), verification (per-statement entailment results), and final disposition (answered / abstained / escalated). Store traces in a queryable store so RAGChecker-style attribution and FP1-FP7 labeling can be computed offline from traces alone.

Evaluation: add RGB-style robustness suites (noise, negative rejection, information integration, counterfactual evidence) and claim-level diagnostics (RAGChecker/FActScore: claim recall, context utilization, noise sensitivity, hallucination rate) to the CI harness; these separate retriever faults from generator faults, which the RAGAS triad cannot do. Gate generator-model upgrades on negative-rejection and noise-sensitivity regressions, not only on faithfulness.

Chunking governance: start from fixed-size chunks with contextual prefixes and treat structure-aware or semantic chunking as an A/B experiment measured on the real corpus (Qu et al. found semantic chunking's cost unjustified in general). Make chunking a versioned index parameter with a documented evaluation result attached to each index version.

Ordering policy as configuration: support both relevance-edge ordering (Lost in the Middle, LongLLMLingua) and order-preserving packing (OP-RAG), selected per DomainProfile and plan, and validate the choice with the position-sensitivity test on every generator change; do not hard-code a single ordering heuristic.

Knowledge-conflict handling: add an Astute-RAG-style consolidation step that groups claims by source and surfaces contradictions (e.g. between spec revisions) instead of silently resolving them; weight newer document versions and higher-trust sources, and abstain when no consistent group is backed by trusted retrieved sources.

Cost control via model tiering: use speculative drafting (small drafters over evidence subsets, frontier model only verifies) for high-volume SINGLE_STEP traffic, distilled rerankers (RankGPT permutation distillation) instead of LLM rerankers at steady state, and late chunking instead of per-chunk LLM prefixes for very large corpora where the $1/M-token contextualization cost is prohibitive.

Fine-tuning path when weights are available: adopt the RAFT / Yoran et al. distractor-mixed recipe (synthetic in-domain QA, oracle plus distractors, a fraction with no oracle, verbatim-quote chain-of-thought) with about 1,000-5,000 examples per domain, and retrain embedding models with DPR-style hard negatives mined from production queries; schedule retraining with index re-versioning.

Freshness and staleness: time-stamp every chunk and expose recency as both a metadata filter and a trust signal; run a scheduled freshness evaluation using time-sensitive questions (Atlas-style index update tests) and alert when answers cite superseded document versions.

Multi-hop retrieval option: offer a graph-walk retriever (HippoRAG Personalized PageRank over an entity graph, seeded from existing traceability links where possible) as a cheaper single-call alternative to the IRCoT loop for multi-entity trace questions, selected by the router when two or more distinct entities are detected.

Release process: canary new index versions and new retriever/reranker models on a traffic slice with side-by-side claim-level metrics before promoting the alias; keep the previous index version hot for instant rollback; and require a reproducibility record (index version, model versions, prompt version, DomainProfile hash) on every stored answer so incidents can be replayed against the exact configuration that produced them.
pitfalls: Missing content answered anyway (Barnett FP1): the corpus lacks the answer but the model fabricates one. Mitigate with a corrective gate (CRAG INCORRECT branch), explicit abstention instructions, selective augmentation that returns no evidence (RECOMP), and abstention-rate monitoring.

Gold document ranked below top-k (Barnett FP2): mitigate with hybrid BM25+dense, contextual chunking, query fan-out with RRF, and rerank depth 150 -> 20 (Anthropic: -67% failures); measure recall@k against labeled sets.

Retrieved but lost in consolidation or ignored in the middle (Barnett FP3; Liu et al. 'Lost in the Middle'): accuracy drops from 75.8% to 53.8% when the gold passage moves from position 1 to 10. Mitigate with reranking, best-first/second-best-last ordering, compression to a budget, and capping evidence near 20 chunks.

Answer in context but not extracted (Barnett FP4): noise or contradictions distract the model. Mitigate with knowledge-strip refinement (CRAG), extractive compression, prompts that license ignoring irrelevant text, and RA-DIT-style fine-tuning when weights are available.
Wrong output format (Barnett FP5): mitigate with schema-constrained generation, validators and one repair retry.
Incorrect specificity and incomplete answers (Barnett FP6/FP7): mitigate with TaskSpec capturing the required granularity, completeness judges, and multi-step plans for multi-part questions.

Over-retrieval and over-compute on simple queries (Adaptive-RAG; Self-RAG motivation): fixed k retrieval for every query wastes cost and can hurt accuracy (no-retrieval beat single-step on GPT-3.5 F1). Mitigate with complexity routing and a retrieval trigger threshold.

RAG failure categories under long-context comparison (Li et al. 2024): multi-step reasoning, general queries, long/complex queries, implicit whole-context queries. Mitigate with IRCoT loops, GraphRAG/RAPTOR for global queries, and Self-Route escalation to long context.
Compression trades citation recall for correctness (ALCE SUMM/SNIPPET: citation recall 73.6 -> 68.9/65.3): keep source-span pointers and prefer extractive compression when citations are mandatory.
Incomplete citation support even in strong models (ALCE: best models lack full support ~50% on ELI5): verify with NLI and regenerate; never trust self-reported citations.
Hallucinated hypothetical documents in HyDE and over-abstraction in Step-Back for domain-private entities: gate these transforms behind a domain-knowledge flag and measure their marginal recall.
Hard-coded thresholds that do not transfer (CRAG thresholds vary from (0.59,-0.99) to (0.95,-0.91) across datasets): calibrate per domain on a labeled set and re-calibrate on model change.

Unreliable automatic judges, especially context relevance (RAGAS 0.70 human agreement) and uncalibrated LLM scores: use ARES-style fine-tuned judges with PPI and human-labeled validation sets; treat scores comparatively.
Expensive index rebuilds and silent staleness (Barnett; GraphRAG/RAPTOR indexing cost): version indexes, rebuild incrementally, and expose index version in every trace and cache key.
Runaway agentic loops and ungoverned autonomy (Singh et al.): enforce step/token budgets, deterministic fallbacks and audit logs.
Validation only feasible in operation (Barnett): do not ship on offline benchmarks alone; sample live traffic for judge scoring and human review from day one.
evaluation_metrics: Retrieval: recall@k and gold-in-top-k (k=5,10,20), MRR/nDCG@10 against labeled or synthetic query-passage pairs; retrieval failure rate at top-20 (Anthropic reports 5.7% -> 1.9%)
Post-consolidation gold-in-context rate (Barnett FP3) and context relevance (RAGAS: fraction of context sentences needed)
Faithfulness / groundedness (RAGAS statement-level support; 0.95 human agreement), answer faithfulness (ARES judge with PPI confidence intervals)
Answer relevance (RAGAS question-regeneration cosine; ARES judge) and task correctness (EM/F1/accuracy on domain QA sets; FactScore-style for long-form)
Citation recall and citation precision via NLI (ALCE/TRUE), plus fraction of statements with at least one citation
Abstention metrics: abstention rate, abstention precision (correctly declined unanswerable) and recall (missed unanswerables), Self-Route 'unanswerable' fraction
Routing metrics: plan distribution, escalation rate, router accuracy against cheapest-successful-plan labels, cost per plan
Efficiency: end-to-end latency p50/p95, tokens per query (input/output), compression ratio, relative time vs single-step (Adaptive-RAG style), cost per 1,000 queries
Position-sensitivity test: accuracy as a function of gold-passage position (U-shape magnitude, Liu et al.)
Format compliance: schema validation pass rate and repair-retry rate (FP5)
Completeness and specificity judges (FP6/FP7) on sampled traffic; human preference win rates for comprehensiveness/diversity on global questions (GraphRAG protocol)
Failure-point attribution distribution (FP1-FP7) over time as a drift and regression signal; judge-human agreement (Kendall tau, pairwise accuracy) re-measured per domain
engineering_adaptation_notes: Code: chunk by syntactic unit (function/class/module) with a contextual prefix naming file path, module and purpose; index symbols and identifiers with BM25 (exact match matters more than semantics); use extractive compression only (never token-dropping on code); add a code-symbol index (LSP/ctags) as an additional retriever fused via RRF; verify claims by compiling/running or by NLI against the exact span.

Specifications and standards: long, hierarchical documents suit RAPTOR trees seeded by heading structure; retain clause/section IDs as metadata and in the contextual prefix; step-back queries map naturally to 'which clause/principle governs this'; citations must resolve to clause numbers and revision/version.

Requirements and traceability: store requirement ID, parent/child links, verification method and status as metadata; multi-step IRCoT plans implement trace queries (requirement -> design -> test -> incident); GraphRAG entity graphs can be built directly from existing traceability links instead of LLM extraction, cutting indexing cost.

Test logs and telemetry: high-volume, repetitive, structured text; pre-aggregate (dedupe stack traces, cluster failures) before indexing; BM25 on error codes dominates; time-window metadata filters are essential; compression should be extractive and preserve numbers and timestamps exactly.

Incident reports and postmortems: narrative sources where abstractive compression and GraphRAG community summaries (themes, recurring root causes across incidents) add value; global plan for 'what patterns recur', single-step for 'what happened in INC-1234'; completeness judges matter because postmortems are multi-part.

CAD/BOM metadata: mostly tabular; route to structured/SQL retrieval tools with the LLM generating filters rather than embeddings over flattened rows; embed only descriptive fields; fuse structured results with document chunks through the same Evidence interface; citation = row/part ID and revision.

Domain profiles should set: chunk policy, metadata schema, retriever weights (lexical heavier for identifiers), gate thresholds calibrated on 100-300 labeled queries, compression mode, citation strictness, judge prompts, and the corpus-size gate for whole-corpus caching of small manuals or standards.

Security and governance: metadata-level access control enforced at retrieval (pre-filter), PII/secret redaction before indexing, audit logs of evidence used per answer, and versioned indexes so an answer can be reproduced against the index snapshot it used.
composition_notes: Hybrid retrieval: Pipeline RAG is the orchestrator and hybrid retrieval is its retrieval operator; this dossier's defaults (contextual chunking, BM25+dense, RRF k=60, rerank 150 -> 20) define the contract the hybrid retrieval component must honor, and the query fan-out stage supplies it multiple queries plus metadata filters. The retrieval component owns index versioning; the pipeline owns the corpus-size gate and the decision to call it at all.

Task decomposition: the router's MULTI_STEP plan and IRCoT loop are where decomposition plugs in; the decomposition component turns a complex prompt into sub-questions, each executed as one retrieve-and-reason hop, and its DAG also drives the parallel branches of a GraphRAG map step. Step-back abstraction is a decomposition primitive (specific -> principle) shared between the two components.

Answer verification: Self-RAG IsSup/IsUse judgments, CRAG evidence scoring, ALCE citation precision/recall and the RAGAS/ARES triad are the verification component's inputs and outputs; the pipeline exposes statements, citations and source spans so verification can run NLI, and consumes verification results to regenerate, filter or abstain (self-consistency style multi-sample verification composes at the generation stage).

Parallelization: query variants, per-retriever searches, per-chunk evaluator scoring, REPLUG-style parallel generations over evidence subsets, and GraphRAG map steps over community reports are all embarrassingly parallel fan-out/fan-in points; the parallelization component should provide a bounded fan-out primitive with fusion (RRF or score aggregation) and a global token/latency budget.

Caching: cache rewrites by normalized query, retrieval results by (query variant, index version, filters), contextual prefixes and summaries by chunk hash, and final answers by semantic similarity with an index-version check; prompt caching of a whole corpus under ~200K tokens replaces retrieval entirely (Anthropic: >2x latency and up to 90% cost reduction) and is the cheapest plan the router can select.

Prompting and architecture best practices: use structured outputs for router/rewriter/judge stages, instruct the generator that evidence may be irrelevant, place instructions and the best evidence at the context edges (Lost in the Middle), keep system prompts and domain profiles cacheable prefixes, bound agentic loops with explicit budgets, and run offline+online evaluation with calibrated judges so every configuration change is measured against the failure-point taxonomy.
critique_corrections: RECOMP entry mixes compressors. The dossier states 'NQ EM 39.39 -> 37.04, TriviaQA 62.37 -> 58.68, HotpotQA 32.80 -> 30.40 (extractive)'. In RECOMP Table 2 (Flan-UL2), 37.04 (NQ, 36 tokens) and 58.68 (TriviaQA, 32 tokens) are the ABSTRACTIVE compressor results; the extractive compressor gives NQ 36.57 (37 tokens) and TriviaQA 58.99 (38 tokens). Only HotpotQA 30.40 (75 tokens) is extractive; abstractive HotpotQA is 28.20 (64 tokens). Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2310.04408.

Adaptive-RAG 'Label distribution: 8.6% A, 53.3% B, 38.1% C' is mislabeled. These figures (8.60 / 53.33 / 38.07, Table 3) are the distribution of the classifier's PREDICTED labels on test queries, not the training-label distribution; the paper does not report training-label proportions (400 queries sampled per dataset). The technique's 'expect roughly 9% NO / 53% SINGLE / 38% MULTI' should be described as the test-time routing distribution on six open-domain QA datasets. Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2403.14403.

ARES: 'applies prediction-powered inference with ~150 human-annotated points' understates the main setting. ARES used 300 human annotations in its main experiments and 200 for the AIS experiments; ~150 is reported as the approximate minimum needed (Table 3). Also, ARES does not report a Kendall tau for answer faithfulness (only context relevance 0.91 and answer relevance 0.97 on real systems); faithfulness was evaluated separately on AIS with judge accuracy. Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2311.09476.

GraphRAG: 'root-level C0 still wins 72%/62% while using 9-43x fewer context tokens than source-text map-reduce'. Per Table 6/Figure 2, C0 vs vector RAG wins ~72% comprehensiveness on both Podcast and News, but diversity is ~77% on Podcast and ~62% on News (62% is News only). The 9x-43x range in the Table 2 caption spans community levels (C1 through C0); C0 alone uses about 38x (Podcast: 26,657 vs 1,014,611 tokens) and 43x (News: 39,770 vs 1,707,694) fewer tokens than source-text summarization. Source: https://arxiv.org/html/2404.16130.

GraphRAG technique default '1 gleaning pass (more for recall-critical corpora)' is not a paper-reported setting.
